q: Among any six people, show that there are three who all know each other, or three who are all strangers to each other.
How many rectangles (of any size) are there on an $8 \times 8$ chessboard? How many squares?

A path goes from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ in unit steps, each step being either $R$ (right, $(1,0)$) or $U$ (up, $(0,1)$). (i) Show that there are $\binom{2n}{n}$ paths. (ii) By considering where a path meets the line $x+y=n$, prove that $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^2=\binom{2n}{n}$. (iii) Call a path bad if it visits some point strictly above the line $y=x$. By reflecting part of a bad path in the line $y=x+1$, show that the number of bad paths is $\binom{2n}{n-1}$. (iv) Deduce that the number of paths that never go above $y=x$ is $\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$, and check your answer for $n=3$ by listing the paths.

(i) How many of the integers $1,2,\ldots,1000$ are divisible by none of $2$, $3$ and $5$? (ii) A derangement of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is a permutation with no fixed point. Show that the number of derangements is $D_n = n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$. (iii) Compute $D_4$ and $D_5$. (iv) At a Secret Santa, $n$ people draw names at random. Find the limit, as $n\to\infty$, of the probability that nobody draws their own name. (v) Prove that $D_n=(n-1)(D_{n-1}+D_{n-2})$ for $n\ge 3$.

Prove each identity by counting something in two ways, where possible. (i) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}=2^n$. (ii) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}k\binom{n}{k}=n2^{n-1}$. (iii) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}=0$ for $n\ge 1$. Deduce that a set of size $n\ge 1$ has equally many subsets of even and odd size. (iv) $\sum_{k=0}^{n}k^2\binom{n}{k}=n(n+1)2^{n-2}$. (v) By integrating $(1+x)^n$, evaluate $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{n}{k}$.

There are $m$ different presents and $n$ children. (i) In how many ways can the presents be given out (with no restrictions)? (ii) If $m\le n$, in how many ways can they be given out so that no child gets more than one? (iii) In how many ways can 4 presents be given to 3 children so that every child gets at least one? Answer this directly, and by inclusion-exclusion. (iv) Show that the number of ways to give out $m$ presents so every child gets at least one is $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)^m$. (v) Deduce that $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)^n=n!$, and that the same sum with exponent $m<n$ is $0$.

A necklace has beads at the vertices of a regular polygon, each coloured with one of $n$ colours. Two necklaces are the same if one is a rotation of the other. (i) How many ways are there to colour the corners of a square with 2 colours, if the square is fixed in place? How many different necklaces are there? (ii) Let $p$ be prime. Show that a colouring of a $p$-bead necklace that is not all one colour has exactly $p$ different rotations. (iii) Deduce that there are $n+\frac{n^p-n}{p}$ different $p$-bead necklaces, and hence that $p$ divides $n^p-n$. (iv) Find the number of different 6-bead necklaces with 2 colours. Why does the formula in (iii) not apply?
A stick of length 1 is broken at two points, chosen independently and uniformly at random along its length. What is the probability that the three pieces can be arranged to form a triangle?
